cards.t: A stranger knocks at Wuthering Heights
cards.b: In 1801 Mr Lockwood, a fussy gentleman from the south, rents Thrushcross Grange, a comfortable house on the Yorkshire moors. His landlord, Heathcliff, lives four miles away at Wuthering Heights, a bleak farmhouse battered by wind. Lockwood visits and finds a household seething with hostility: the dark, savage Heathcliff; a beautiful, scornful young widow called Cathy; Hareton Earnshaw, an unschooled, sullen young farmhand; and Joseph, a sour old servant forever quoting scripture. Nobody explains who anyone is, and Lockwood, puzzled and a little frightened, blunders from one social mistake to the next.

Trapped overnight by a snowstorm, Lockwood is put in an old oak-panelled box bed. Scratched on the window ledge he finds three names: Catherine Earnshaw, Catherine Heathcliff, Catherine Linton. In a nightmare, an icy child's hand grips his through the broken pane and a voice sobs, "Let me in!" claiming to have been a waif for twenty years. He screams. Heathcliff rushes in, sends him out, then wrenches open the window and begs the ghost to come to him. Back at the Grange, Lockwood asks his housekeeper, Nelly Dean, to tell him everything.

Nelly's story begins about thirty years earlier, when she was a servant at the Heights. Old Mr Earnshaw returns from Liverpool with a ragged, dark-skinned orphan found starving in the streets. He names him Heathcliff, after a son who died, and openly favours him. His own children react very differently. Wild, bold Catherine quickly becomes Heathcliff's inseparable companion, but her older brother Hindley sees the boy as a usurper and bullies him. When Mr Earnshaw dies, Hindley comes home from college with a wife, Frances, and takes cruel revenge by reducing Heathcliff to a farm labourer.

Degraded and denied schooling, Heathcliff clings to Catherine, and the two run half-wild across the moors together. One Sunday night they creep to Thrushcross Grange and peer through the window at the spoiled Linton children, Edgar and Isabella, quarrelling over a lapdog in a crimson drawing room. A bulldog seizes Catherine's ankle. The Lintons take her in as a young lady but throw Heathcliff out as a gypsy brat. Catherine stays five weeks and comes home elegantly dressed and mannered. Beside her, the dirty Heathcliff feels humiliated, and Edgar mocks him openly.

In 1778 Frances gives birth to a son, Hareton, and dies soon after of consumption. Hindley, wild with grief, sinks into drinking, gambling and violence; servants leave, the curate stops calling, and once he nearly kills baby Hareton by dropping him over the banisters, saved only when Heathcliff catches him by reflex. Heathcliff grows more brutish and silent under Hindley's tyranny and tells Nelly he is only planning how to pay Hindley back. Meanwhile Edgar Linton, gentle and well-bred, begins visiting, and Catherine starts behaving differently to suit each of her two companions.

Edgar proposes and Catherine accepts. That night in the kitchen she confides to Nelly that she has no business marrying Edgar: in her soul she knows she is wrong. Her dream of heaven ends with her weeping to return to the Heights. But Hindley has brought Heathcliff so low, she says, that it would degrade her to marry him. Heathcliff, sitting unseen behind the settle, hears this and slips away, missing what follows: that he is more herself than she is. He disappears into the stormy night. Catherine searches for him, soaked, and falls dangerously ill with fever.

cards.t: Two souls made of the same stuff
cards.q: He's more myself than I am. Whatever our souls are made of, his and mine are the same.
cards.b: Catherine speaks these words to Nelly in Chapter 9, just moments after Heathcliff has walked out believing she despises him. It is the novel's hinge: a love so total it erases the line between two people, spoken at the exact instant that love is lost through bad timing, pride and class.

Three years later Catherine is married to Edgar and living at Thrushcross Grange. The household is calm, even happy, until Heathcliff reappears, now tall, well dressed and mysteriously rich. Nobody learns where he has been. He lodges at the Heights with Hindley, feeds his drinking and gambling, and steadily wins his property. Catherine is overjoyed to see him; Edgar is cold and wary. Edgar's sister Isabella, eighteen and romantic, falls hopelessly in love with Heathcliff, who sees in her only a weapon: she is her brother's heir.

Catherine warns Isabella that Heathcliff is a fierce, pitiless, wolfish man, but Isabella will not listen. When Edgar finds Heathcliff kissing Isabella and orders him out, a violent quarrel breaks out; Catherine locks herself in her room, refuses food for three days and falls into delirium, pulling feathers from her pillow and longing for the moors of her girlhood. That same night Heathcliff elopes with Isabella. At the Heights he treats his bride with calculated cruelty, even hanging her little dog on the way, and she soon writes to Nelly in despair.

Catherine never fully recovers. Pregnant and wasting, she receives Heathcliff one last time while Edgar is at church. Their meeting is less tender than ferocious: they cling together, accuse each other of breaking their hearts, and weep. That night Catherine gives birth two months early to a daughter, also named Catherine (called Cathy), and dies without regaining her senses. Heathcliff, who has waited all night in the garden, dashes his head against a tree and prays that she will haunt him in any form: he cannot live without his life, his soul.

Isabella escapes the Heights and flees south, where she gives birth to a sickly son, Linton Heathcliff. Six months after Catherine's funeral Hindley drinks himself to death, so mortgaged that Heathcliff now owns Wuthering Heights outright. He keeps young Hareton there and raises him as an illiterate labourer, deliberately repeating exactly what Hindley once did to him, though the boy grows oddly fond of his tormentor. Edgar, grieving, withdraws from the world to raise Cathy at the Grange, where she grows up spirited, loving and kept entirely ignorant of the Heights.

When Cathy is about thirteen, Isabella dies and Edgar brings home her son Linton, a pale, peevish invalid. Heathcliff immediately claims him, despising him but plotting to marry him to Cathy and so secure the Linton estate. Cathy wanders to the Heights, laughs at Hareton because he cannot read his own name over the door, and befriends Linton. Edgar forbids the visits, so the cousins exchange secret love letters and Cathy sneaks out at night. Linton, terrified of his father and quickly dying of consumption, becomes the bait in Heathcliff's trap.

As Edgar lies dying, Heathcliff lures Cathy and Nelly into the Heights and locks them in. He strikes Cathy, and holds them for days until she marries Linton. She escapes just in time to reach her father's bedside before he dies. Heathcliff has also bribed Edgar's lawyer, so the will cannot be changed to protect her. Cathy is forced back to the Heights to nurse Linton, who dies soon after, having willed everything to his father. Heathcliff now owns both houses, and Cathy is a penniless, embittered widow. This is the household Lockwood stumbled into.

cards.t: New life and a final haunting
cards.b: Lockwood leaves, then returns in 1802 to find the Heights transformed. Cathy has begun teaching Hareton to read, and the two young people have fallen in love. Heathcliff, his revenge within reach, finds he no longer wants it: in both their faces he sees Catherine's eyes. Haunted by her presence everywhere, he stops eating and sleeping. One morning Nelly finds him dead in the oak-panelled bed, the window swinging open in the rain. He is buried beside Catherine. Cathy and Hareton will marry, and Lockwood wonders how anyone could imagine unquiet slumbers beneath that quiet earth.

Heathcliff is the most magnetic and frightening lover in English fiction. Brought in as an outsider, scorned for his class and colour, he turns his humiliation into a lifelong project of revenge, hurting children who never wronged him. Yet his grief for Catherine is so raw that we cannot simply hate him. Brontë asks us to hold both truths at once.

Catherine is proud, passionate, wilful and generous by turns. She loves Heathcliff as her own self, yet chooses Edgar for comfort, status and a fine house. She wants to keep both men, and the moors and the drawing room, without paying for either. Her tragedy is that she cannot become one person, and the split literally kills her.

Most of the story comes to us through Nelly, the sensible, warm-hearted housekeeper. She seems trustworthy, but read closely: she keeps secrets, carries letters, takes sides, and sometimes nudges events toward disaster. Brontë uses her to remind us that every story we hear about other people's lives has been filtered through someone's loyalties and judgements.

Catherine and Heathcliff's love is not sweet or courtly. It is closer to a shared identity, almost a single soul in two bodies. Brontë shows how glorious and how dangerous such love is: it makes ordinary marriage, kindness and compromise look pale, and when it is thwarted it turns destructive, consuming everyone nearby.

Hindley degrades Heathcliff; Heathcliff degrades Hareton; abused children grow into abusers. The novel is built in two generations so that we can watch harm being passed down like property. Only when Cathy and Hareton choose patience and teaching over contempt does the cycle break, and the house, at last, can breathe.

The two houses stand for two ways of living. Wuthering Heights is storm, earth, instinct and rough honesty; Thrushcross Grange is carpets, books, manners and comfort, but also softness and snobbery. Brontë refuses to crown either one. The happy ending joins the best of both: Hareton's strength and Cathy's learning.

cards.t: Do not act on half a sentence
cards.b: Heathcliff hears Catherine say marrying him would degrade her, and leaves before she says he is more herself than she is. Three lives are wrecked by a half-heard conversation. When something you overhear wounds you, stay and ask. The rest of the sentence is often the part that matters.

Catherine marries Edgar while admitting her soul says no. Trying to keep comfort and passion at once, she ends up with neither. Big decisions about who you share your life with deserve honesty with yourself, even when the honest answer is inconvenient or less respectable.

Heathcliff spends twenty years seizing both houses and humbling his enemies' children. When he finally holds everything, he finds he cannot enjoy it and no longer even wants it. Getting even rarely heals the original wound; it only drags more people into it, including ourselves.

Heathcliff treats Hareton exactly as Hindley treated him, proof that we tend to repeat what was done to us. Notice the habits of anger or contempt you absorbed growing up. Recognising them is the first step to being the person in your family line who stops passing them on.

cards.t: Contempt closes doors; teaching opens them
cards.b: Young Cathy first laughs at Hareton for not reading his own name, and he burns his books in shame. Later she sits beside him and teaches him patiently, and love grows from it. Mockery makes people defensive; helping them learn makes them grow.

cards.t: Status is a poor reason to marry
cards.b: Catherine chooses Edgar partly because he will be rich and she will be the greatest woman in the neighbourhood. Isabella chooses Heathcliff for a romantic fantasy. Both marriages are miserable. Look past money, polish and glamour to character and real compatibility.

cards.t: Grief needs a way to move
cards.b: Heathcliff refuses to let Catherine go for eighteen years, even opening her coffin, and his frozen grief poisons everything around him. Mourning deeply is human; building your whole life around a loss is not. Let grief change you without letting it rule you.

Wuthering Heights shows hurt passing from one person to the next until someone chooses to stop it. Think of a sharp word, a habit of coldness, or a grudge that was handed to you by someone else. Who might receive it from you next, and what would it take for you to be the one who lets it end?
